academic.title: Task 1 · Bicycle travel in three towns
academic.instructions: The graph shows the percentage of journeys to work made by bicycle in three fictional towns between 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words. Spend about 20 minutes on this task.
academic.model:
The line graph compares the proportion of journeys to work made by bicycle in three towns over a twenty-year period. Overall, cycling became more common in Alder and Brook, whereas Cedar experienced a gradual decline. Alder recorded the largest increase and finished with the highest percentage.
In 2005, Cedar led the three towns at 30%, followed by Alder at 10% and Brook at 5%. Alder's figure then rose steadily, reaching 20% in 2015 and 35% by 2025. This represented a gain of twenty-five percentage points across the period. Brook also increased throughout, although more slowly, from 5% to 20%.
By contrast, the share in Cedar fell to 25% in 2015 and 20% in the final year. Alder overtook Cedar between 2015 and 2020, while Brook caught up with Cedar only at the end. Thus, despite starting with the lowest proportion, Brook matched the former leader in 2025, and Alder finished fifteen percentage points ahead of both.
academic.analysis: The overview identifies both directions and the final ranking. Comparisons use percentage points correctly. No cause is invented for the trends.
rubric: Task achievement / response: address the task and develop relevant material.
Coherence and cohesion: organise and connect ideas clearly.
Lexical resource: select precise, appropriate vocabulary.
Grammar: use a useful range of structures with control.

visual.alt: Line graph of bicycle commuting. Years 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025. Alder: 10,15,20,30,35 percent. Brook: 5,8,12,16,20. Cedar: 30,28,25,22,20.

academic.title: Task 2 · University learning
academic.instructions: Some people believe universities should require every student to study a subject outside their main area of specialisation. Others think students should focus entirely on their chosen subject. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons and relevant examples. Write at least 250 words. Spend about 40 minutes on this task.
academic.model:
Universities must decide how to balance depth of knowledge with a broader education. Requiring students to take a subject outside their main specialisation can widen their perspective, while a fully focused programme leaves more time for demanding professional knowledge. In my view, a limited and carefully designed requirement offers the better balance.
There are sound reasons to protect specialist study time. Some programmes already contain a large amount of essential material, and students need opportunities to practise rather than merely encounter it. An engineering student, for example, may benefit more from completing a substantial design project than from attending an unrelated introductory course chosen only to satisfy a rule. Additional requirements can also create timetable conflicts and financial pressure if they extend the length of a degree.
Nevertheless, another field can help students recognise assumptions within their own. A computing student who studies ethics may ask more careful questions about the consequences of collecting personal data. Equally, a literature student taking an introductory statistics course may become better equipped to assess numerical claims. Such learning is valuable when the connection is explained and the course is accessible to non-specialists. It is less useful if students enter an advanced class without the necessary background.
I would therefore support one modest requirement with a range of suitable choices. Universities should ensure that it fits within the normal programme and invite students to explain how the additional subject informs their main work. This would preserve depth while creating a real opportunity for broader thought. The goal should be meaningful intellectual contact between fields, rather than simply adding another examination to an already crowded schedule.
academic.analysis: Both views receive a reasoned paragraph. The position is qualified and consistent. The examples illustrate reasoning rather than claim research findings.
rubric: Task achievement / response: address the task and develop relevant material.
Coherence and cohesion: organise and connect ideas clearly.
Lexical resource: select precise, appropriate vocabulary.
Grammar: use a useful range of structures with control.

general.title: Task 1 · Letter to a course coordinator
general.instructions: You recently completed an evening course at a local centre. The practical sessions were useful, but a change to the timetable caused difficulties. Write a letter to the course coordinator. Describe what you found useful; explain the problem caused by the timetable change; suggest an improvement for future courses. Begin “Dear Sir or Madam”. Write at least 150 words. Do not write an address. Spend about 20 minutes.
general.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing about the beginners' bicycle maintenance course that I completed at your centre last week. I found the practical sessions particularly valuable because the tutor allowed us to work on our own bicycles and checked each stage of the process. I now feel more confident carrying out basic checks safely.
However, moving the last two meetings from Wednesday to Monday caused a difficulty. I work until seven on Mondays, so I missed the beginning of both sessions. The change was announced only a few days beforehand, which gave me little opportunity to rearrange my shifts. As a result, I had to ask classmates to explain material they had already practised.
For future courses, I would suggest keeping the advertised timetable wherever possible. If a change is unavoidable, please give participants more notice and offer a short replacement session or clear demonstration notes. These arrangements would help learners benefit fully from an otherwise excellent course.
Yours faithfully,
Alex Morgan
general.analysis: All three bullet points are covered with concrete detail. The formal opening and closing match an unknown recipient. The suggestion is realistic rather than a demand for an unrelated benefit.
rubric: Task achievement / response: address the task and develop relevant material.
Coherence and cohesion: organise and connect ideas clearly.
Lexical resource: select precise, appropriate vocabulary.
Grammar: use a useful range of structures with control.

general.title: Task 2 · Local facilities
general.instructions: Some people think local authorities should spend more money on public parks, while others believe indoor sports facilities should be the priority. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words. Spend about 40 minutes.
general.model:
Local authorities often have to choose between several worthwhile uses of a limited leisure budget. Public parks provide flexible outdoor space, while indoor sports facilities support activities that depend on equipment or protection from the weather. I believe existing access and local needs should guide the choice, with basic public park provision protected in every neighbourhood.
Parks can serve many purposes without requiring visitors to join an organised activity. People may walk, rest, play with children or meet friends. A well-maintained park can therefore benefit residents whose ages, incomes and interests differ. Free entry is particularly important where households cannot afford regular membership fees. However, an attractive space still needs ongoing care, safe paths and suitable access; simply setting aside land does not guarantee a useful park.
Indoor facilities also have a strong case. A swimming pool, for instance, cannot be replaced by an open field, and a sports hall can host activities throughout a wet winter. Such places may provide structured lessons and opportunities for people to develop specific skills. Their limitations are cost and reach. Construction and operation can be expensive, and a facility with high charges may serve a relatively narrow group unless affordable sessions are available.
In my opinion, councils should first examine which residents currently lack usable facilities. In an area with little green space, improving a local park may be more urgent than constructing another hall. Elsewhere, an accessible indoor centre may fill a genuine gap. Funding decisions should also include maintenance and affordable access, rather than focus only on an impressive opening. A balanced programme based on actual need is more defensible than treating one type of facility as the automatic priority everywhere.
general.analysis: The essay compares practical benefits and limits, then gives a conditional position. Each paragraph develops a point; the conclusion does not introduce a new claim.
rubric: Task achievement / response: address the task and develop relevant material.
Coherence and cohesion: organise and connect ideas clearly.

toefl.title: Write an Email · Room booking problem
toefl.instructions: You lead a student project group. A room you reserved for Thursday at 4 pm has become unavailable. Your group needs a quiet room with a screen for a visiting adviser. Write an email to the activities coordinator, Ms Patel. Explain the situation, describe what the group needs, and propose a workable alternative or ask about availability. You have 7 minutes. Write in complete sentences; no official minimum word count is imposed in this practice task.
toefl.model:
Dear Ms Patel,
I am writing about the room our project group reserved for Thursday at 4 pm. We have been told that it is no longer available, but our visiting adviser has already arranged to meet us at that time.
We need a quiet space for six people with a screen so that we can show our draft design. Could you check whether another room with these facilities is free? If none is available at four, we could begin at four thirty, provided the adviser agrees. We would need to confirm that change with her today.
Please let me know which option is possible and whether we should make a new booking ourselves. Thank you for helping us find an alternative.
Best regards,
Sam Lee
toefl.analysis: The email covers all three communicative requirements, distinguishes a possible alternative from a confirmed change, and makes an actionable request.
rubric: Communicative purpose: address all three email requirements with appropriate requests and register.
Elaboration: include relevant, useful details and make the next action clear.
Organisation: connect the message clearly for its intended reader.
Language: control grammar, word choice, spelling and conventions while using an appropriate range.

toefl.title: Write for an Academic Discussion · Campus funding
toefl.instructions:
Professor Chen: A university has a small fund for improving student life. Should it spend the money on extending library hours or supporting more student-led social activities? Explain your view.

Mina: Longer library hours would help students who work during the day and need a quiet place in the evening.

Carlos: Social activities help new students build relationships, so I would fund groups that welcome people who do not already know one another.

Contribute your own supported opinion to the discussion. An effective response will generally contain at least 100 words. You have 10 minutes.
toefl.model: I would prioritise longer library hours if the university can first show that students are being turned away from suitable study space. Mina makes a strong point about students with daytime jobs: an evening opening could improve access without requiring them to change their work schedule. However, opening an entire building may be expensive. The university could begin by extending access to one staffed study area and review how it is used. I agree with Carlos that social connections matter, but student groups might receive practical support, such as free rooms and publicity, even without a large cash grant. A small trial would allow the university to respond to evidence rather than assume that either option benefits everyone equally.
toefl.analysis: The contribution engages with both classmates while adding a practical, supported proposal. It is an illustrative response, not an awarded ETS score.
rubric: Contribution: express a relevant, supported opinion in the discussion.
Elaboration: develop reasons or examples and add your own contribution rather than copying classmates.
Organisation: connect ideas clearly within the available response.
Language: use varied syntax and precise vocabulary with appropriate control.

b2.title: Part 1 · Compulsory essay
b2.instructions:
Your English class has discussed how towns can encourage people to walk more. Your teacher asks you to write an essay.
Question: What is the best way to encourage people to walk for everyday journeys?
Write about: 1. safe routes; 2. public information; 3. your own idea.
Give reasons for your opinion. Write 140–190 words in an appropriate style.
b2.model:
Encouraging people to walk requires more than telling them that walking is beneficial. In my view, safe and convenient routes should be the first priority, supported by useful information.
Firstly, people are unlikely to walk regularly if a journey involves narrow pavements or a dangerous crossing. Improving these basic conditions can make an everyday trip feel realistic, especially for families and older residents. An attractive campaign cannot compensate for a route that people are afraid to use.
Secondly, information can help when it answers practical questions. A clear map showing walking times and suitable crossings is more useful than a general slogan. However, it must reflect the actual condition of the streets.
My own suggestion is to provide places to rest. A bench can make a longer route manageable for someone who needs a pause, and it also makes the street more welcoming.
Overall, towns should remove practical barriers before expecting publicity to change habits. Safe paths, clear guidance and resting places can work together to make walking an ordinary choice.
b2.analysis: All three required points, including an original third idea, are developed in an essay register.
rubric: Content: address the task and inform the target reader.
Communicative achievement: use an appropriate register and genre.
Organisation: connect and structure the text.
Language: use a range of vocabulary and grammar with control.

b2.title: Part 2 · Article
b2.instructions: A local English-language magazine asks: “A useful skill”. Write an article describing a practical skill you have learned. Explain how you learned it and why other people might enjoy trying it. Give your article a title. Write 140–190 words.
b2.model:
A repair worth learning
What do you do when a favourite shirt loses a button? Until recently, I put it in a drawer and promised to deal with it later. Learning a little sewing finally changed that habit.
I began at a community class, where the tutor showed us how to make a secure stitch. Watching was helpful, but actually trying it revealed the difficult parts. My first button was attached at a strange angle. After some advice and another attempt, it sat properly. I practised on an old shirt before touching anything valuable.
The pleasure is not only saving money. A small repair allows you to keep using something you like, and the result is easy to see. You do not need a whole room of equipment to begin.
If you would like to try, choose a simple project and ask an experienced person to check your method. One successful repair will not make you an expert, but it may rescue a garment and give you the confidence to learn the next step.
b2.analysis: The title, direct question and engaging register suit a magazine article; both required explanations are present.
rubric: Content: address the task and inform the target reader.
Communicative achievement: use an appropriate register and genre.
Organisation: connect and structure the text.
Language: use a range of vocabulary and grammar with control.

b2.title: Part 2 · Email
b2.instructions: You receive an email from your English-speaking friend Jamie: “I am visiting your town for a day next month. What could we do together? I like being outdoors, but we need a plan if it rains. Let me know what you suggest and what I should bring.” Write your email. Write 140–190 words.
b2.model:
Hi Jamie,
It is great that you are coming next month! I would love to spend the day with you. If the weather is dry, we could walk along the river and have a picnic in the park. The path is fairly level, and there are plenty of places to stop, so we would have time to talk rather than rush.
If it rains, there is a small local museum near the station. It has an interesting display about how the town developed, and the cafe next door would be a good place for lunch. I will check the opening times before your visit so we do not arrive at a closed door.
Bring comfortable shoes and a light waterproof jacket. You will not need to carry picnic food because I can prepare that here. Let me know what time your train arrives, and I will meet you outside the main entrance.
I am really looking forward to seeing you!
Best,
Alex
b2.analysis: The informal register suits a friend. It proposes both weather options, gives reasons and answers what to bring.
rubric: Content: address the task and inform the target reader.
Communicative achievement: use an appropriate register and genre.
Organisation: connect and structure the text.
Language: use a range of vocabulary and grammar with control.

b2.title: Part 2 · Review
b2.instructions: An English-language website wants reviews of places where people can spend a free afternoon. Review a place you know. Describe what visitors can do, explain one limitation and say who would enjoy it most. Give your review a title. Write 140–190 words.
b2.model:
A quiet afternoon at the town museum
If you want an interesting afternoon without buying an expensive ticket, the town museum is worth considering. Its permanent collection is free, and it is small enough to explore without feeling overwhelmed.
The best section shows photographs of streets as they looked a century ago. You can compare them with a modern map and discover familiar places behind very different shopfronts. There are also recordings of residents describing work and family life. I found these personal accounts more memorable than the display of old tools.
The main limitation is the lack of space to sit. Visitors who want to listen to every recording may need a break in the cafe next door, where food and drinks are charged separately. Checking the current opening hours is also sensible.
I would recommend the museum especially to people who enjoy local history and careful observation. It may not suit someone seeking an active or noisy afternoon, but it offers plenty to discuss afterwards.
b2.analysis: The review balances specific description, a limitation and a target audience rather than only listing attractions.
rubric: Content: address the task and inform the target reader.
Communicative achievement: use an appropriate register and genre.
Organisation: connect and structure the text.
Language: use a range of vocabulary and grammar with control.

ieltsSpeaking.title: Part 2 · Long turn
ieltsSpeaking.instructions: You have one minute to prepare and up to two minutes to speak. Make brief notes during preparation.
prompts: Describe a time when you learned something useful from another person.
Say who the person was, what you learned, and how the learning happened.
Explain why the experience was useful to you.
ieltsSpeaking.model:
I would like to describe learning how to maintain my bicycle from a neighbour. I had used the bicycle for months, but I did not know how to check it properly. When the chain began making a noise, I assumed I needed an expensive repair.
My neighbour first asked me to explain when the noise happened. Then he showed me a few simple checks and let me do them while he watched. That was more useful than just watching him fix it, because I discovered which steps I did not understand. He also explained which problems I should leave to a qualified mechanic.
Afterwards, I wrote a short checklist and used it the following weekend without help. The experience was useful because it made me more confident without making me overconfident. I could handle basic care and describe a problem clearly when I needed advice. It also changed how I learn practical things: I now try to practise a step myself and ask for feedback rather than assume that understanding a demonstration means I can do it.
ieltsSpeaking.analysis: The answer establishes a specific event, develops the process and reflects on its value. It is an illustrative long turn, not an examiner-awarded band.
rubric: Fluency and coherence: sustain a connected and relevant response.
Vocabulary: communicate precise meaning and paraphrase when needed.
Grammar: vary structures with control.
Pronunciation: use intelligible sounds, stress, rhythm and intonation.

ieltsSpeaking.title: Part 3 · Learning and society
ieltsSpeaking.instructions: Discuss the broader questions. In a live IELTS test an examiner selects and follows up questions; this timed solo set cannot assess interactive performance.
prompts: What makes an explanation easy to understand?
How do practical skills and academic knowledge support each other?
Should schools teach more everyday skills? Why?
Can videos replace learning from a teacher?
How might adults be encouraged to continue learning?
ieltsSpeaking.model: Videos can be very useful for reviewing a familiar procedure because the learner can pause or replay them. However, they cannot always diagnose why a particular learner is struggling. A teacher can observe an attempt and adapt the explanation. I would therefore combine the two when possible: use a clear video for preparation, then practise with feedback. The balance depends on the skill and the consequences of making a mistake. A simple craft project and a hazardous technical procedure should not be treated in the same way.
ieltsSpeaking.analysis: This sample develops one discussion question by distinguishing cases and supporting a qualified view.
rubric: Fluency and coherence: sustain a connected and relevant response.
Vocabulary: communicate precise meaning and paraphrase when needed.

What skills might the people need?
b2Speaking.model: Both photographs show people taking part in an activity together, but the kind of coordination seems different. b2Speaking.title: Part 3 · Collaborative discussion
b2Speaking.instructions: Work with a partner. Discuss the question for two minutes, then use the next one-minute stage to reach a decision. In solo rehearsal, practise possible contributions; interaction remains unassessed.
prompts: A town wants to help new residents get to know one another. How useful might these ideas be?

b2Speaking.title: Part 4 · Further discussion
b2Speaking.instructions: Discuss these questions with a partner or tutor for about four minutes. Solo rehearsal does not provide an interactive-communication score.
prompts: Why can it be difficult to meet people after moving?
Do organised activities help everyone equally?
How can local groups make newcomers feel welcome?
Is meeting online as useful as meeting in person?
Who should support community activities?
b2Speaking.model: Organised activities can help because they provide a reason to start talking. However, people may be unable to attend at the advertised time or may feel uncertain about the activity. Offering clear information, a friendly first contact and a choice of events could make participation easier.
b2Speaking.analysis: Develop answers and engage with another speaker. A tutor should assess discourse management and interactive communication as well as language.
